messages.content: Can you research whether we should switch our dental clinic's appointment reminder system? We keep getting no-shows and the front desk thinks the software is the problem.

Before searching anything, that question needs to be taken apart, because "should we switch" hides at least five separate questions, and only some of them are about software:

1. What is our actual no-show rate, and how does it break down (new vs. returning patients, day of week, booking lead time)? Without a baseline, no switch can be judged.
2. What does the evidence say about reminder type — text vs. call vs. email — and timing? This is the one part web research answers well.
3. What do the alternative systems cost, and do they integrate with our scheduling software, or would the front desk be double-entering?
4. What are the consent and opt-out rules for texting patients reminders in our state? A system that texts without proper consent is a liability, not a fix.
5. Is the no-show pattern actually a reminder problem at all — or a booking-policy problem (no deposit, overbooking habits, long lead times)?

What would change my mind about the whole project: if sub-question 1 shows no-shows cluster on long-lead-time bookings regardless of reminders sent, the fix is policy, not software, and I'd tell you to stop shopping.

If you can tell me your current no-show rate (even a rough monthly figure), I'll start with sub-question 2 and work outward. If you can't, sub-question 1 becomes the first research task, and it comes from your own records, not the web.
Research standing desks for me — are they actually healthier? Everyone in the office wants one now.

"Are standing desks healthier" is not one question, and most of the content online answers a blurrier version of it. Here is the decomposition I'd research against:

1. Healthier for what outcome? Back pain, cardiovascular markers, calorie burn, and afternoon alertness are different claims with different evidence. A desk can help one and do nothing for the others.
2. Standing all day vs. sit-stand alternation? Almost all the plausible benefit sits in alternating; prolonged static standing has its own documented downsides (leg and vein strain). These get conflated constantly.
3. What do studies actually measure, and for how long? A two-week study measuring self-reported comfort is not evidence about long-term health.
4. What's the effect size? "Statistically detectable" and "worth $600 per employee" are different bars.
5. Who shouldn't stand more? Any guidance that ignores existing joint or circulation issues is marketing, not research.

What would change my mind: a well-run longer-term study showing sit-stand desks produce no measurable difference on any of the outcomes in question 1 — at that point the honest recommendation is "buy them for comfort and preference if you like, but not as a health intervention."

Tell me which outcome your office actually cares about and I'll weight the research toward it instead of producing a generic pros-and-cons list.
Our bakery's ingredient delivery bills are way up this year. Find out why.

I'll break that into pieces before searching: (1) which ingredients drove the increase — flour, butter, eggs, and sugar move independently; (2) is it commodity prices, delivery/fuel surcharges, or our supplier's margin; (3) did our order pattern change (smaller, more frequent orders cost more per unit)? A general web search can only speak to piece 1 and part of piece 2, so let me see what it gives us — and I'll be explicit about what it can't settle.

arguments.query: food ingredient wholesale price increases 2026 flour butter eggs

messages.name: web_search
messages.content:
1. National food-service price roundup (industry newsletter, Oct 2026): wholesale food prices up 6.1% year over year on average; eggs and dairy named as the largest movers.
2. Commodity market explainer (agriculture news site, Sep 2026): wheat futures roughly flat on the year after a spring spike that later reversed.
3. Supplier blog post (regional distributor): cites fuel surcharges and minimum-order changes across the industry.
4. Statistics agency release: food-at-home and food-away-from-home indices both up, dairy sub-index up 9.4%.

Here is what that search does and doesn't establish. It supports a real background increase — dairy up about 9.4% on the agency index, wholesale food overall up 6.1% — and wheat/flour looks roughly flat after a spring spike reversed, so flour is probably not your driver. The distributor's mention of fuel surcharges and minimum-order changes is a lead, not evidence: it's a supplier explaining its own prices.

What the web cannot tell us is your split. Your actual answer lives in your invoices: line-item prices for butter and eggs this year vs. last, the delivery fee line, and your order frequency. If your butter price rose ~9% but your bill rose 25%, the gap is surcharges, minimums, or order pattern — all negotiable or fixable, unlike commodity prices.

Next step, if you want it: give me two or three invoices from this year and the same months last year and I'll decompose the increase exactly. Searching more general articles would just repeat the averages we already have.
Our landlord just told us we can put a sign on the roof of our shop. I have a meeting with a sign company in two hours — can you check whether that's actually allowed?

With two hours, this becomes a different research job than it would be with two days, and it's worth saying how:

The two-hour plan (what I'll do now):
1. Find the municipal sign ordinance itself — the actual code section on roof signs, not a sign company's summary of it. One primary source beats ten articles.
2. Check whether our zoning district or any historic-district overlay changes the rule for this address.
3. Check whether a permit is required and what it asks for (structural review is common for roof signs).
Stop rule: the moment I have the code text and the permit requirement, I stop. You need a yes/no-with-conditions for the meeting, not a literature review.

The two-day plan would add: how the rule has been enforced on comparable buildings nearby, the appeal/variance process and its timeline, and quotes interpreted against the code. None of that changes what you say in two hours, so none of it belongs in this pass.

One caution to carry into the meeting: the landlord's permission is necessary but not sufficient — landlords regularly grant things the city prohibits. If the sign company says "we do these all the time," ask them for the permit path in writing; the code, not their experience, is what counts.
We're thinking of opening a second coffee shop across town. Research whether it's a good idea.

"Good idea" decomposes into questions with very different sources, so here's my plan before I search anything:

1. Demand: foot traffic and demographics near the candidate area (web research helps here).
2. Cost: commercial rents for comparable spaces (listings are a start; a broker's actuals are better).
3. Cannibalization: how much of the new shop's trade would come from our existing customers rather than new ones — that's our own sales/postcode data, not the web.
4. Staffing: can we hire and train a second crew without diluting the first shop? Mostly an internal question.
5. Capital: fit-out cost and the cash buffer afterward — our own numbers.

What would change my mind: if the rent data shows the area priced for chains rather than independents, the location fails on cost regardless of demand. Let me start with the piece the web answers best — the demand picture.

arguments.query: neighborhood foot traffic demographics retail study east side district

messages.name: web_search
messages.content:
1. City economic development profile (2025): the east side district added 1,900 housing units in three years; median household income slightly above city average.
2. Local news article (Aug 2026): two national coffee chains announced east side locations opening next spring.
3. Commercial property listing roundup: asking rents in the district up 14% in a year, vacancy under 5%.
4. University urban-studies blog: foot traffic counts on the main corridor doubled since 2023, driven by a new transit stop.

First pass, with the receipts and their limits:

Demand looks real — 1,900 new housing units, rising foot traffic since the transit stop opened (city profile and a university study agree, and they're independent sources). But the same pass surfaces the two risks my plan flagged: two national chains are opening there next spring, and asking rents are already up 14% with under 5% vacancy — the district is being priced for exactly the competitors who are coming.

What this doesn't settle: cannibalization (needs your customer postcode data), staffing, and whether actual signed rents match asking rents. My honest interim read: demand — yes; timing and price — questionable. The next research step isn't more web searching; it's your sales data for question 3 and a broker conversation for real rent actuals. I'll write up the full claim-by-claim version whenever you're ready.
Pick the best CRM for our nonprofit — we have 12 staff and we're drowning in spreadsheets.

I won't search yet, because "best CRM" searches return affiliate roundups written for commissions, and they'll happily crown a winner that lacks the one thing nonprofits actually need. Criteria first:

1. Donor management, not just contacts: gift history, recurring donations, thank-you/acknowledgment workflow. This is where generic business CRMs fail nonprofits.
2. Price at 12 seats, including the nonprofit discount — several vendors give 50%+ to nonprofits, which reshuffles the ranking entirely.
3. Migration: can it import our spreadsheets without a consultant?
4. Who administers it? With no IT staff, setup complexity is a real cost.
5. Reporting for the board and for grant applications.

Now I'll run one search — not to pick a winner, but to see what the roundup landscape claims, treating it as a list of candidates to verify against vendor documentation, never as evidence.

arguments.query: best CRM for small nonprofits 2026 donor management

messages.name: web_search
messages.content:
1. Software roundup site: ranks five CRMs, top pick praised for 'powerful sales pipelines'; article contains affiliate links (disclosed at the bottom).
2. Second roundup site: different top pick; scoring criteria listed as 'features, ease of use, value' with no donor-management category.
3. Vendor's own page: claims 'built for nonprofits' with donor tracking and acknowledgment letters.
4. Nonprofit technology forum thread: practitioners warn that two popular CRMs charge extra for the donation module.

As predicted, the roundups are a candidate list, not an answer. Notice what the search actually gave us: roundup #1's top pick is praised for sales pipelines — a criterion that doesn't appear on ours — and neither roundup scores donor management at all. The forum thread is the most useful item: practitioners flagging that donation features are a paid add-on in two popular products is a concrete, checkable claim.

The research path from here: take the four or five candidate products, and for each one verify against the vendor's own documentation (a) donor module included or add-on, (b) 12-seat price with nonprofit discount, (c) spreadsheet import path. That's primary-source work; the roundups have done all they can do. If you tell me whether you need event registration and volunteer tracking too, I'll finalize the candidate list and start the verification pass.
Our subscription box service is losing customers. Research why churn is up.

Churn research fails when it starts by collecting opinions. It works when it starts with rival hypotheses and asks what evidence would separate them. Here are the live candidates and their fingerprints:

H1. Price sensitivity (a competitor undercut us, or our last increase landed badly). Fingerprint: churn concentrated in the cohort that got the increase; exit reasons mention cost; signups still healthy.
H2. Onboarding failure (new customers never reach the "good" experience). Fingerprint: churn concentrated in months 1–2; long-tenured customers stable.
H3. Product fatigue (the box got repetitive). Fingerprint: churn rising with tenure; engagement with each box declining before cancellation.
H4. A specific bad experience (a shipping failure, a quality incident). Fingerprint: a step-change in churn starting at a datable event, not a gradual slope.
H5. Market-wide pressure (category shrinking). Fingerprint: competitors showing the same pattern in public data — this is the only hypothesis web research can test directly.

What would change my mind about where to dig: the shape of your churn curve by tenure. If it's H2-shaped, all the competitor research in the world is wasted effort; if it's a step-change, we go hunting for the event.

So the honest sequence: first, your own cohort data (which needs no searching at all), and only then web research aimed at whichever hypothesis survives. Tell me what your churn-by-tenure looks like, even roughly, and I'll aim the research instead of spraying it.
Deadline is Friday — is our community garden eligible for the county green-spaces grant? Quick answer needed.

Time-boxed question, so the plan is narrow: find the county's own program page, extract its eligibility criteria, and check the garden against each one. No background reading, no similar-programs detour. Stop the moment each criterion is matched or failed.

arguments.query: county green spaces grant eligibility community gardens

messages.name: web_search
messages.content: County Green Spaces Program — official program page (updated Jan 2026). Eligibility: (1) applicant must be a registered nonprofit or a fiscally sponsored community group; (2) site must be publicly accessible at least 20 hours per week; (3) site must be within county boundaries and on land with written landowner permission for 5+ years; (4) grants of $2,000–$15,000 for soil, water access, fencing, and tools; (5) applications close the last Friday of the month.

Against the county's own criteria — the only source that counts for eligibility:

1. Registered nonprofit or fiscally sponsored group — NEEDS CHECKING on your side. If the garden is an informal group with no sponsor, this is the blocker, and it's fixable: fiscal sponsorship through an existing nonprofit is explicitly allowed.
2. Public access 20+ hours/week — your unlocked daylight-hours garden likely meets this, but "likely" should become a stated schedule in the application.
3. Landowner permission for 5+ years in writing — NEEDS CHECKING. A verbal OK from the landowner is not what the criterion says.
4. Budget range and covered items match typical garden needs.
5. Deadline: last Friday of the month — consistent with your Friday deadline.

Verdict: eligible on the program's terms if items 1 and 3 are in order. Those are paperwork facts only you can confirm, and no amount of additional searching substitutes for them. If both check out, apply; the two open items are also exactly what a reviewer would flag.
Is solar worth it for the roof of our warehouse? Give me the research plan before you start.

Here's the plan, and notice how little of it is generic web content — solar economics are brutally specific to your roof, your tariff, and this year's incentive rules:

1. The roof itself: age, remaining life, orientation, shading, structural capacity. If the roof needs replacement within about five years, the project usually dies here — you'd pay to remove and reinstall the array. This is the first question, not the last.
2. Your load profile: warehouses that use power during daylight self-consume far more than they export, and self-consumed power is worth the retail rate while exported power earns much less. Your last 12 months of bills are the primary source.
3. Incentives as of now: tax credits and local programs change and expire; anything I find must carry a date and come from the program administrator, not an installer's summary.
4. The arithmetic: installed cost per watt for commercial rooftops (comparable quotes, not national averages), payback under your tariff, and sensitivity — what happens to payback if export compensation drops.
5. Installer quotes as primary documents: three quotes, compared line by line, are worth more than any article.

What would change my mind mid-research: learning the roof is near end-of-life (stop, sequence the re-roof first), or that your tariff pays near-retail for exports (which makes the case much stronger than typical).

Give me the roof's age and a year of electricity bills and I'll run this in order.
Can you research AI tools for our team? We want to be more efficient.

I can, but as stated, that brief would produce the internet's default answer — a listicle of forty tools — and it would waste your time. "AI tools" only becomes researchable when it's tied to tasks. Here's the decomposition I'd propose, and the three questions that would sharpen it:

Decomposition by task, not by product:
1. Drafting and summarizing (documents, emails, meeting notes) — the most mature category.
2. Data work (cleaning spreadsheets, pulling reports) — where accuracy failures are costly and demos mislead.
3. Customer-facing replies — where tone and error risk matter most, and where I'd be most conservative.
4. Search across your own files — valuable only if your documents are organized enough to search.

Evaluation criteria I'd apply to any candidate: does it work on YOUR data (not the demo's), what does it do with your data (retention and training policies, from the vendor's actual policy documents), per-seat cost at your team size, and exit cost if you stop.

The three sharpening questions:
1. Which task eats the most skilled-person hours right now? That's where a pilot pays.
2. What data would the tool touch — anything confidential or regulated?
3. Who would run a two-week pilot and judge it against a defined "better"?

What would change my mind about scope: if the answer to question 1 is one specific painful task, we research three tools for that task deeply instead of forty tools shallowly — depth wins. Answer those three and I'll come back with a short, verified shortlist instead of a catalog.
We're in a cold climate — will a heat pump actually keep our house warm at -15°C? Research it.
First pass with the obvious query, knowing what it usually returns:

arguments.query: heat pump reviews best

messages.name: web_search
messages.content:
1. 'Top 10 Heat Pumps of 2026' — review roundup site; rankings based on features and price, no low-temperature test data.
2. 'Heat Pumps: The Ultimate Buying Guide' — retailer content blog; recommends its own stocked brands.
3. 'We Tested 14 Heat Pumps' — affiliate review site; tests conducted at mild temperatures, methodology not stated.
4. Manufacturer marketing page: 'reliable warmth all winter' with no numbers.

That set is unusable for your question — it's optimized for selling, contains no low-temperature performance data, and two of the four are retailers. Refinement 1: add the technical quantity that actually answers the question — COP (coefficient of performance) at the temperature you care about. This excludes listicles because they never publish COP tables.

arguments.query: cold climate heat pump COP at -15C performance data

messages.name: web_search
messages.content:
1. Regional energy-efficiency program page: table of certified cold-climate models with COP at -15°C ranging 1.8–2.4, and capacity retention 70–85% of rated output.
2. HVAC trade article: explains capacity drop-off and backup heat sizing, with example curves.
3. University extension explainer: heat pumps in northern climates, references the same certification table.

Better — real numbers now. Refinement 2: go for the primary document itself, the manufacturer's engineering datasheet, using the exact phrase engineers use. This excludes everyone summarizing and leaves the source the certifiers themselves work from.

arguments.query: "coefficient of performance" heat pump datasheet "-15" capacity table

messages.name: web_search
messages.content: Manufacturer engineering datasheet (PDF, rev. 2025): model line's COP at -15°C = 2.1; heating capacity at -15°C = 76% of nominal; minimum operating temperature -25°C; defrost cycle notes included.

Now the question is answerable, and notice the path: roundup filler → certification data → primary datasheet. The datasheet says this model line delivers a COP of 2.1 at -15°C (still twice as efficient as resistance heat) but only 76% of its nominal capacity — so the real design question is sizing and backup heat for the coldest nights, not whether the technology works. The certification table agrees (COP 1.8–2.4 across models), so two independent kinds of source line up. What would still need a local installer: your home's heat-loss calculation, which no search can do.
Find the actual rule on whether we can put a sign on our shop's roof. We're in the City of Alden.
Starting broad to see the landscape, expecting blogs:

arguments.query: can I put a sign on my building roof

messages.name: web_search
messages.content:
1. Sign company blog: 'Roof signs make a bold statement — here's what to know' (no jurisdiction, no code citations).
2. General legal Q&A site: answers vary by city; mentions permits in passing.
3. Forum thread: anecdotes from three different states, mutually contradictory.
As expected: no jurisdiction, no citations, contradictions. Refinement 1: name the kind of document that governs this — the municipal code — which pushes blogs down and code repositories up.

arguments.query: roof sign permit municipal code requirements

messages.name: web_search
messages.content:
1. Model municipal code library: sample ordinance language on roof signs (a template, not Alden's law).
2. Neighboring city's code, section on signs: roof signs prohibited above the roofline in commercial districts.
3. Sign-industry article summarizing typical municipal approaches.

Closer, but a template and a neighbor's code are not Alden's rule — a very common research trap is answering from the wrong jurisdiction's document because it ranked well. Refinement 2: bind the query to Alden itself and the code's own vocabulary.

arguments.query: City of Alden municipal code signs roof sign section

messages.name: web_search
messages.content: City of Alden Municipal Code, Title 17, Section 17.42.060 — Signs: 'Roof signs are permitted in the C-2 district only, shall not extend more than 6 feet above the roof surface, and require a sign permit with structural certification by a licensed engineer. Roof signs are prohibited in the H historic overlay district.' District map linked from the same page.

That's the primary source, and it answers precisely: in Alden, roof signs are allowed only in the C-2 district, capped at 6 feet above the roof, with a permit and an engineer's structural certification — and banned outright in the historic overlay. Two checks remain, and they're about your address, not the rule: which district your shop sits in (the linked map answers it), and whether the historic overlay touches your block. What made the difference across the three queries: first naming the document type (municipal code), then naming the jurisdiction — each refinement excluded a class of wrong answers, not just added keywords.
I heard a rumor that the magnetic building tiles my kids have were recalled. Can you check?
Rumors plus product names produce news noise first — watch what each refinement does:

arguments.query: magnetic building tiles recall

messages.name: web_search
messages.content:
1. News story (2024): a different brand of magnetic tiles recalled two years ago.
2. Parenting blog: 'Are magnetic tiles safe?' — general safety discussion, no recall notice.
3. Retailer listing page for the tiles, no safety notice shown.

Nothing there is about your set, and a 2024 recall of a different brand is exactly how rumors mutate. Refinement: add the year and the name of the only body whose recall notices are authoritative — the federal product-safety regulator — so we get notices, not commentary.

arguments.query: magnetic tile set recall 2026 consumer product safety commission notice

messages.name: web_search
messages.content: Regulator recall notice database entry (dated March 2026): one magnetic tile set — sold under a specific import brand name — recalled for magnet loosening; remedy is a refund; notice lists the model numbers and the sales window (Nov 2025–Feb 2026). No other magnetic tile sets appear in the 2026 notices.

Now it's checkable against the physical object, which is where recall research should always end up. The regulator's March 2026 notice covers one specific import brand and lists model numbers and a Nov 2025–Feb 2026 sales window. So: check the brand name and model number on your box. If they match the notice, stop using the set and follow the refund remedy in the notice. If your set is a different brand or bought outside that window, this notice doesn't cover it — and no other 2026 notice covers magnetic tiles. The refinement that mattered was adding the regulator's name and the year: it converted a rumor into a document you can match against a label.

I searched 'when was the old mill in Hartfield built' and got junk: a real-estate listing mentioning the mill, two tourism pages saying 'historic mill' with no date, and a page selling mill-themed wedding packages. I just want the year it was built.

Those results failed for a specific reason: your query reads like a question a tourist asks, so the engine served tourist and commercial pages. The mill's construction year lives in different kinds of documents — local-history society pages, newspaper archives, and property/county records — and you reach them by searching the way those documents are written.

Refinements to try, in order:

1. Exact phrase: "Hartfield mill" "built in" — pages that state a year usually use that phrasing; this one change often ends the search.
2. Add the document type: Hartfield mill history historical society — steers toward the local-history society, the single most likely holder of a dated account.
3. Add the mill's other names: mills often appear under a founder's name ("gristmill" plus the family name if you know it) — older documents use "gristmill," not "mill."
4. If a tourism page mentions a fire or a rebuild, search that event: "Hartfield mill" fire — mills were frequently rebuilt, and 'built' may have two true answers (original and current structure), which is worth knowing before you cite a year.

What to trust when you find it: a dated history-society account or a newspaper item outranks any tourism page, and if two dates appear, check whether one is the founding and the other the current building. Run refinement 1 first — I'd expect it to finish this in one step.
Our invoicing program keeps dying with 'Error 0x2F7A: ledger segment fault on commit'. Find out what it means and whether there's a fix.
Error-string research has one golden rule: the exact string is the query. But let me show the contrast — first, the natural-language version people usually try:

arguments.query: invoicing program crashes when saving invoice error

messages.name: web_search
messages.content:
1. Generic troubleshooting article: '10 reasons software crashes' — reinstall, update drivers, check disk space.
2. Forum thread about a different program's save crash from 2021.
3. Antivirus vendor blog suggesting crashes are often malware.
Zero signal, as expected — paraphrase matches everything and nothing. Refinement 1: the exact error string, quoted, which only matches pages containing that literal text:

arguments.query: "ledger segment fault on commit"

messages.name: web_search
messages.content:
1. Vendor knowledge-base article KB-2291: 'Error 0x2F7A on commit occurs when an invoice batch contains a credit note referencing a deleted tax code; fixed in version 7.3.2; workaround: reassign the credit note's tax code before committing.'
2. User forum thread (vendor's own forum): three users confirm the KB workaround; one reports it also triggers from archived tax codes.

One quoted query replaced three useless results with the vendor's own knowledge base. Refinement 2 would be adding your version number to confirm the fix applies to you — the KB says fixed in 7.3.2, so if you're on 7.3.2 or later and still seeing it, the forum's note about archived tax codes is the next lead, and that distinction matters before you change anything.

Answer with receipts: KB-2291 (primary, vendor) identifies the cause — a credit note pointing at a deleted tax code — and gives both a fix (update past 7.3.2) and a workaround (reassign the tax code first). The forum thread is corroboration from users, weaker than the KB but consistent with it. Check your version number; that's the fork in the road.
Does turmeric actually help with joint pain? I keep seeing it everywhere.
The phrasing of the question determines the quality of what comes back. First, the question as asked:

arguments.query: does turmeric help joint pain

messages.name: web_search
messages.content:
1. Supplement brand's blog: 'Turmeric: nature's answer to joint pain!' with a shop link.
2. Wellness magazine: '9 foods that fight inflammation,' turmeric at #3, no studies cited.
3. Influencer post summarizing the magazine article.

That's a marketing echo chamber — a brand, a listicle citing nothing, and a post citing the listicle. Refinement 1: ask for the evidence type instead of opinions. Systematic reviews sit atop the evidence hierarchy because they aggregate the trials:

arguments.query: curcumin osteoarthritis systematic review meta-analysis randomized trials

messages.name: web_search
messages.content:
1. Systematic review (2024, medical journal): pooled 11 randomized trials of curcumin extracts for knee osteoarthritis; found modest pain-score improvements vs. placebo, smaller than standard painkillers; noted most trials were short (under 4 months) and several were industry-funded.
2. Evidence-summary page from a national health institute: describes the same literature as 'promising but limited,' flagging small sample sizes.

Now there's something to actually say, and notice how different it is from the blogs. The systematic review's honest summary: curcumin extracts show a modest benefit for knee osteoarthritis pain in trials — smaller than standard painkillers, mostly short trials, some industry-funded. The health institute's summary independently characterizes the evidence as promising but limited, which is corroboration of the *characterization*, not of a miracle.

Two lessons to keep: (1) changing the query from 'does X help' to 'systematic review of X' moved us from sellers to evidence; (2) the answer the evidence supports is narrow — a specific extract, a specific joint, a modest effect — and anything broader than that is the marketing talking. Whether it's appropriate for you personally is a question for your doctor, especially alongside other medication; that's outside what research can settle.
What R-value does the code require for attic insulation here? We're in climate zone 5.
First pass, broad:

arguments.query: attic insulation R-value recommended

messages.name: web_search
messages.content:
1. Insulation manufacturer's guide: recommends R-49 to R-60 'for most attics' — a sales-oriented range covering several zones.
2. Home-improvement article: 'Most homes need R-38' with no zone mentioned.
3. Forum debate: posters in different states citing different numbers as 'the code.'

Three different numbers because the question mixes up a recommendation with a requirement, and a national answer with a zonal one. Refinement: name the code and the table — residential energy codes publish ceiling R-values by climate zone, and that's the document a building inspector works from:

arguments.query: residential energy code ceiling insulation R-value table climate zone 5

messages.name: web_search
messages.content:
1. Energy code table (residential provisions): climate zone 5 ceiling requirement listed as R-49 for new construction under the current edition; R-38 shown for an earlier edition.
2. State energy office page: confirms the state adopted the current edition with amendments; attic retrofits in existing homes treated under a separate existing-buildings chapter.

The refinement exposed a fork the broad search hid: R-49 (current edition, new construction) vs. R-38 (earlier edition) — and a second fork between new construction and retrofit of an existing attic, which the state energy office says is governed separately. So the correct answer is conditional: if this is new construction in zone 5 under the current code edition, R-49; if you're adding insulation to an existing home, the existing-buildings chapter applies and I should pull that table instead — tell me which case you're in. The manufacturer's 'R-49 to R-60' range wasn't wrong, exactly; it was answering 'what's good' when you asked 'what's required,' and those are different documents.

I searched for the best time of year to visit the coast near Port Sable and every result is a travel site saying 'September is a hidden gem!' with hotel ads. I want actual weather patterns, not marketing.

You've diagnosed it correctly: 'best time to visit' is a commercial query, and search engines answer commercial queries with commercial pages. The data you want exists — it's just published as climate statistics, not travel content. Refine toward the documents, not the destination:

1. Search for climate normals: Port Sable climate normals monthly temperature precipitation — weather services publish 30-year monthly averages (temperature, rainfall, rainy days) for named stations. That's the raw material for your own judgment.
2. Add the specific variable you care about: if you hate rain, search rainy days by month; if you care about sea temperature, that's a separate dataset (oceanographic agencies publish monthly sea-surface averages). 'Best' hides which variable matters — name yours.
3. For storm risk, search the historical record: tropical storm landfalls near Port Sable by month — emergency-management and weather-service pages keep these counts, and they're ad-free.

How to read what you find: prefer the station data tables over any prose summary, check which 30-year period the normals cover (they're updated roughly every decade, and an old set will read slightly cooler/drier), and treat any single 'best month' claim — even from a good source — as someone else's weighting of the variables. With the normals table in front of you, you can weight them yourself: pick your month by the rain column, the temperature column, or the storm column, and know exactly what you traded away.
How accurate is the GlucoTrack G7 continuous glucose monitor? I want the real accuracy figure, not ads.
Starting where a shopper starts, to show why it fails:

arguments.query: GlucoTrack G7 reviews accuracy

messages.name: web_search
messages.content:

How long should a tank water heater last? Search and tell me which sources I should actually trust.

arguments.query: how long does a tank water heater last years

messages.name: web_search
messages.content:
Search results (8):
1. Manufacturer's product documentation page: warranty terms list 6- and 12-year tank warranties by model; an anode-rod maintenance schedule in the manual.
2. Plumbing standards institute explainer: service life discussion citing field data, tank heaters typically 8–12 years.
3. Utility company customer page: 'expect 8–12 years; sediment flushing extends life.'
4. Regional newspaper home column: quotes two local plumbers, 'about a decade.'
5. National plumbing company's blog: '10–15 years' and a prominent 'book a replacement' button.
6. Content aggregator ('HomeFactsDaily'): 'Water heaters last 15–20 years!' — no author, no date, no sources.
7. Discussion forum thread: owners reporting anywhere from 5 to 22 years.
8. Listicle farm page ('TopHomeTips'): text closely matching result 6's phrasing, also undated.

Triage of the eight, ranked by kind — because the ranking is the answer to 'which should I trust':

Tier 1 — primary/technical: (1) the manufacturer's own documentation. Warranty terms (6 or 12 years by model) are a legally meaningful signal of expected life, and the manual's anode-rod schedule tells you life is maintenance-dependent. (2) The plumbing standards institute explainer — institutional, cites field data, says 8–12 years.
Tier 2 — institutional explainer: (3) the utility page. No product to sell you; agrees with tier 1.
Tier 3 — journalism: (4) the newspaper column quoting local plumbers — anecdotal but attributed and dated; consistent with the tiers above.
Tier 4 — interested party: (5) the plumbing company's blog. It sells replacements; its 10–15 is not crazy, but the 'book now' button tells you its incentive.
Tier 5 — anecdote pile: (7) the forum. Useful for the range of real outcomes (5–22 years), useless for the typical figure.
Discarded outright: (6) the aggregator — no author, no date, no sources, and a number (15–20) that contradicts every tier above it; and (8) the listicle farm, which appears to copy (6)'s phrasing, so it isn't even an independent bad source.

Bottom line from the sources that survive triage: plan on 8–12 years for a tank heater, with maintenance (anode rod, flushing) moving you within that range. The discarded pair is a good specimen: the two most confident numbers in the set came from the two sources with nothing behind them.

I found these 8 results about choosing a password manager. Which are worth reading? [1] A password manager vendor's own comparison page where it wins every category. [2] A security researcher's personal blog reviewing three managers, disclosing she was given free licenses. [3] A national consumer magazine's test report — they bought the products and tested them. [4] 'TopPasswordPicks' affiliate site, no author names, every link a referral link. [5] A university IT department's guidance page for its staff. [6] A wire-service news article about a breach at one password manager company last year. [7] A forum thread: 'what does everyone use?' with 200 replies. [8] An undated page, 'Best Password Managers,' listing two products that shut down years ago.

Ranked by kind, with the discards first because they're the easy calls:

Discard outright: (4) the affiliate site — unnamed authors and every link monetized means the ranking *is* the business model; and (8) the undated page — it recommends defunct products, which proves nobody maintains it; an undated page about software is a page that has stopped being true.

Read with a labeled caveat: (1) the vendor's comparison page. Vendors sometimes publish accurate competitor details, but a page where the author wins every category has told you its conclusion in advance — mine it for feature checklists, never for verdicts. (2) The researcher's blog: she discloses the free licenses, which is exactly the honesty signal you want; her testing is one expert's, not a lab's, so it sits below the magazine.

Read first: (3) the consumer magazine's test report — they buy products and test them; that's the closest thing here to a primary evaluation. (5) The university IT page: no sales motive, written for people whose security the institution is responsible for — conservative and practical.

Different job, still valuable: (6) the breach news article isn't a review at all — read it to understand how the company handled an incident, which is a selection criterion no feature chart captures. (7) The forum thread is a popularity poll; skim it only to learn which products have large user communities (support and longevity signals), not which is best.

Order of reading: 3, 5, 2, 6 — and the real lesson is that 'which sources' mattered more than 'which product': four of your eight results couldn't have answered the question no matter what they said.
How fast do EV batteries actually degrade? I want the trustworthy picture, not forum folklore.

arguments.query: EV battery degradation per year capacity loss data

messages.name: web_search
messages.content:
Search results (8):
1. Manufacturer warranty document: battery warranted to retain at least 70% capacity for 8 years/100,000 miles.
2. University battery-lab study (2025): measured fleet of 320 vehicles over 4 years; average capacity loss 1.8% per year, faster in hot climates and with frequent fast charging.
3. Fleet telematics company report: 10,000 vehicles, degradation curves published; averages close to the university study's.
4. National newspaper article: summarizes the university study accurately, quotes an independent engineer.
5. EV enthusiast forum: owners reporting 5% to 25% loss, mixed models and climates, self-selected.
6. Battery-replacement company's page: 'Most EV batteries lose 20% in five years — get a quote.'
7. Content farm page ('EVAnswersHub'): 'EV batteries die in 3 years!' no data, no date.
8. Charging-network blog: 'degradation is a myth' — sells charging subscriptions.

Triage, and note how the incentives line up before the numbers do:

Tier 1 — measurement: (2) the university battery-lab study — 320 vehicles, four years, actual capacity measurements, and it reports the modifiers (heat, fast charging) rather than a single magic number: ~1.8%/year average. (3) The fleet telematics report — 10,000 vehicles of instrumented data from a different organization using a different method, landing in the same place. Two independent measurement programs agreeing is the strongest signal in this set.
Tier 1b — commitment: (1) the warranty document. A guarantee of 70% at 8 years is a floor the manufacturer pays for if wrong — it's a bound, not an estimate, and it's consistent with tier 1's averages.
Tier 2 — faithful summary: (4) the newspaper piece, which reports the study without inflating it.
Anecdote tier: (5) the forum — the spread (5–25%) is real experiences with no controls for climate, model, or charging habits; it tells you variance exists, not what to expect.
Discarded: (6) the replacement company — its 20%-in-five-years figure contradicts both measurement programs and it profits from your believing it; (8) the charging blog's 'myth' claim — same sin, opposite direction, also selling something; (7) the content farm — no data, no date, a claim (3 years) that the warranty document alone refutes.

Trustworthy picture: roughly 1.5–2% capacity loss per year on average, worse with heat and habitual fast charging — and notice that both discarded commercial sources were more dramatic than the data, in opposite directions. Drama is a business model; degradation curves aren't.

We're considering homeschooling and I need the actual notification requirements for our state. Here are my search results — sort them: [1] The state statute itself, Title 22 section on home instruction. [2] The state department of education's 'Home Instruction' FAQ page. [3] A national homeschool advocacy organization's summary of our state's law, with a membership signup. [4] A law firm's blog post, 'Homeschooling in our state: what parents get wrong.' [5] A curriculum company's page: 'Homeschool laws made simple!' selling a compliance checklist. [6] A mom blog recounting her own notification experience three years ago. [7] An undated wiki page summarizing requirements, no citations. [8] A news article about a family fined for missing a notification deadline.

Sorted by what each source is, because for legal requirements the hierarchy is strict:

Tier 1 — the law itself: (1) the statute. This is the only source that *is* the requirement; everything else is commentary about it. Read it first, and read the exact definitions (what counts as notice, to whom, by when, what evidence of progress must be filed).
Tier 1b — the administering agency: (2) the department of education FAQ. Agencies write these to operationalize the statute; where the FAQ and the statute seem to differ, the statute wins, but the FAQ tells you how it's applied in practice (forms, addresses, deadlines as the agency counts them).
Tier 2 — expert commentary: (4) the law firm's post — attorneys summarizing law for marketing, usually accurate on the big points, and useful for 'what parents get wrong,' but verify any deadline against tier 1. (3) The advocacy organization: knowledgeable and often excellent, but it has a membership to sell and sometimes describes what it wishes the law were in edge cases; use it for orientation, confirm against the statute.
Tier 3 — experience and consequence: (6) the mom blog — one family's three-year-old experience; rules and forms change, so treat it as a story about process, not a statement of requirements. (8) The news article — tells you enforcement is real and deadlines bite; not a source of the rules themselves.
Discarded: (5) the curriculum company's 'made simple' page — simplification plus a sales funnel plus legal content is a bad combination; and (7) the undated, uncited wiki — for a deadline-driven legal duty, an undated summary is unusable even if it happens to be right.

Working rule from this set: statute for the requirement, agency FAQ for the procedure, everything else for context. And calendar the deadline from the statute's text, not from anyone's summary of it.

[2] A flour company's recipe blog: 'hooch is normal, just stir it in!' [3] A food-safety agency's general guidance on mold and fermented foods: discard if pink/orange streaks or fuzzy mold appear. [4] A baking influencer's post: 'I revive dead starters all the time, acetone smell means it's just hungry.' [5] A sourdough forum: dozens of conflicting opinions. [6] A content farm article, 'Is sourdough starter dangerous?', no author, stuffed with ads. [7] A microbiology course page explaining starter ecology — acids suppress pathogens. [8] A starter-product company's page selling 'revival kits.'

Sorted, and I'll answer the safety question only from the tiers that earn it:

Tier 1 — food-safety authority: (3) the agency guidance gives you the bright lines: liquid and strong smells are fermentation states; pink/orange discoloration or fuzzy mold means discard. (1) The university extension page is the other tier-1 voice — extension services exist to give exactly this kind of household food-safety guidance, and it agrees with the agency.
Tier 2 — mechanism: (7) the microbiology page explains *why* a healthy starter is hostile to pathogens (acidity) — understanding, not instructions; it supports tier 1 rather than replacing it. (2) The flour company's blog: 'hooch is normal, stir it in' happens to match tier 1, but it's a recipe blog from a seller of flour — right answer, wrong authority; don't generalize from it.

Discarded: (6) the content farm — anonymous, ad-stuffed, exists to rank for your exact anxious query; (8) the revival-kit seller — its advice is inseparable from the product it sells.

Your starter, per tier 1: acetone smell plus liquid on top (hooch) means a hungry starter, not a dangerous one — feed it. Pink/orange streaks or fuzzy mold would mean discard and start over. These results disagree about attic insulation and I can't tell who's credible: [1] The current residential energy code table: zone 5 ceiling R-49. [2] An insulation manufacturer's chart recommending R-49 to R-60 'for most homes.' [3] A state energy office page saying the state adopted the code with an amendment keeping R-38 for existing homes. [4] A home-improvement TV site: 'R-38 is plenty anywhere.' [5] A 2009 forum thread insisting R-30 is code. [6] A utility rebate page: rebates for bringing attics to R-49. [7] An insulation contractor's page saying anything under R-60 is 'basically uninsulated.' [8] An undated aggregator: 'R-value requirements vary,' full stop.

The disagreement dissolves once you sort by kind, because these sources are answering three different questions:

Question 1 — what does the code require? (1) The code table is the primary document: R-49 for zone 5 ceilings under the current edition. (3) The state energy office page is the essential companion: the state adopted that code *with an amendment* — R-38 suffices for existing homes. Both are tier 1, and they're not in conflict: one is the model code, the other is the code as actually adopted where you live. For a legal-requirement question, (3) is the operative source.
Question 2 — what do programs incentivize? (6) The utility rebate page targets R-49 because rebates aim above minimum code. It corroborates that R-49 is the 'good practice' number, but a rebate target is not a legal floor.
Question 3 — what's being sold? (2) The manufacturer's chart and (7) the contractor's page both push above code — R-60 from the people who sell insulation by the bag and by the job. Their numbers may even be cost-effective advice, but they are sales documents and should be read as such. (4) The TV site's 'R-38 anywhere' is the mirror image: a national generalization that ignores zones entirely.
Discarded: (5) the 2009 forum thread — it may have been right about a code edition from 17 years ago, which is precisely why it's wrong now; and (8) the aggregator, whose entire content is that requirements vary — true, empty, and undated.

So: legal minimum for your existing home, per the adopting state: R-38. Good-practice target and rebate threshold: R-49. Anyone quoting you a single number without asking 'new or existing, and which state' is answering a simpler question than yours.

Three articles I've read all say 82% of shoppers check prices on their phones while standing in the store. Is that a real number?
When three articles quote the same oddly precise number, the research task isn't to find a fourth — it's to find the first. Let me pull the chain apart:

arguments.query: "82%" shoppers check prices phone in store

messages.name: web_search
messages.content:
1. Retail trade article (2026): 'A striking 82% of shoppers check prices on their phones in-store, according to research.' Links to article 2.
2. Marketing blog (2025): 'Research shows 82% of shoppers price-check in store.' Links to article 3 as its source.
3. E-commerce platform's blog (2024): '82% of shoppers check prices on mobile while in-store, a survey found.' Names the survey: a retail-technology firm's 'Connected Shopper Survey.'
The chain is visible: the 2026 article cites the 2025 blog, which cites the 2024 blog, which names an actual survey. Two hops of telephone game before we reach anything primary. Now the original:

arguments.query: Connected Shopper Survey retail technology firm methodology sample size

messages.name: web_search
messages.content: Survey report page (retail-technology firm, 2023): 'Connected Shopper Survey — 82% of respondents said they had checked a price on their phone while in a store in the past year.' Methodology note: online survey of 212 shoppers recruited from the firm's own customer panel; fielded October 2023; respondents skewed 25–44 and urban.

Traced to the bottom. The claim as it circulates — '82% of shoppers check prices on their phones in-store' — is not what the original supports. What the 2023 survey actually found: 82% of *its 212 respondents*, recruited from a retail-tech firm's own customer panel (people already engaged with shopping technology), said they had done this *at least once in the past year*. The articles quietly performed three upgrades: a self-selected panel became 'shoppers,' 'in the past year' became a standing habit, and a vendor's marketing survey became 'research.'

The number isn't fabricated — it's inflated by transmission. Usable version: 'In a 2023 vendor survey of 212 panel respondents, 82% reported having price-checked by phone in-store at least once in the previous year.' If your decision needs the real population figure, this source can't carry it, and the honest move is to say so rather than cite the shinier version.
My boss keeps citing that 'remote workers are 13% more productive.' Where does that number actually come from?
A precise percentage repeated for years is a prime candidate for a citation chain. Tracing it:

arguments.query: "13% more productive" remote work study origin

messages.name: web_search
messages.content:
1. HR magazine article (2025): 'Studies show remote workers are 13% more productive.' No citation.
2. Management book excerpt: attributes the 13% figure to 'a famous study at a large travel company.'
3. University research summary page: describes a work-from-home experiment at a large travel agency: call-center employees randomly assigned to work from home showed a 13% performance increase — 9 points from working more minutes, 4 from more calls per minute.
One more step — the study itself, because the summary already hints the headline is a compression:

arguments.query: work from home experiment travel agency call center 13 percent performance attrition

messages.name: web_search
messages.content: Study abstract (economics journal): randomized experiment, 249 call-center volunteers at one travel company over nine months; performance rose 13% (more minutes worked + more calls per minute); attrition fell by half; when the experiment ended and employees could choose, gains roughly doubled — but the authors note results are specific to call-center work that is individual, easily measured, and done by the volunteers who opted in.

Here's what the 13% actually is, and it's a good example of a true number carrying a false implication. The original: 249 *volunteers* in *one company's call center*, doing individual, easily measured work, over nine months. The 13% decomposes into working more minutes (fewer breaks and sick days — about 9 points) and working faster per minute (about 4 points). And the volunteers opted in, which the authors themselves flag.

What your boss's version drops: the job type (call-center work is unusually measurable and solitary), the self-selection, the decomposition (most of the gain was more time at the desk, not superhuman focus), and the fact that one firm in one country a decade ago is a thin base for a universal claim. The number is real; the sentence 'remote workers are 13% more productive' is not what the study says. If it's being used to settle a policy question at your company, the fair citation is: 'in one well-known call-center experiment, output rose 13%, mostly from working more minutes.'

Everyone says the average person checks their phone 144 times a day. I looked into it a bit: the articles I found cite a '2023 mobile usage report,' and when I found that report it turned out to be published by a company that sells phone cases and screen-time apps, based on a survey of its own customers who opted in. Is the number usable at all?

You've already done the trace, and your findings are exactly the ones that determine the answer. Let me formalize what you found, because each fact you uncovered removes a layer of the claim:

1. The source is a vendor, not a research body. A company selling screen-time apps benefits when phone use sounds alarming; that doesn't make its data fake, but it means the framing ('the average person') should be discounted from the start.
2. The sample is its own opted-in customers. People who buy screen-time tools and volunteer for a usage survey are, by construction, people unusually aware of — and likely heavier in — phone use. Generalizing from them to 'the average person' is the core error.
3. 'Checks' was self-reported. Self-reports of habitual behavior are notoriously inaccurate, and this one wasn't validated against device logs, which the report could have used but didn't (or didn't publish).
4. Notice the citation pattern you walked: articles cited 'a 2023 mobile usage report' without naming the company. Vague attribution is often a sign the citer didn't read the source either — they copied it from another article.

Is it usable? In its circulated form, no. In an honest form, barely: 'in a 2023 opt-in survey of one vendor's customers, respondents reported checking their phones an average of 144 times daily.' That's a statement about a self-selected group, not about people. If you need a defensible figure, look for studies that measure device logs rather than ask — they exist, they report lower and more variable numbers, and their methods sections will tell you exactly whose phones were measured. Your instinct to pull the thread was the whole skill: three minutes of 'who says so, and who did they ask' dismantled a number that millions of people repeat.
I keep reading that 40% of food produced never gets eaten. That seems enormous. Trace it for me.
Enormous round numbers deserve a trace. Following the citations:

arguments.query: "40% of food" wasted produced never eaten source

messages.name: web_search
messages.content:
1. Charity campaign page: '40% of all food produced is never eaten.' Cites 'federal estimates.'
2. News article (2025): 'Roughly 40% of the food supply goes uneaten, according to a national food-waste report.'
3. National food-waste report (nonprofit + agency data): estimates 35–40% of the food supply is unsold or uneaten, calculated by weight.
The report is the end of the citation chain — now read what it actually counts, because the methodology section is where the claim lives:

arguments.query: food waste report methodology by weight inedible parts bones peels included

messages.name: web_search
messages.content: Report methodology appendix: the estimate is by weight across the whole supply chain (farm, processing, retail, consumer). It includes inedible parts — bones, peels, pits, coffee grounds — in the 'uneaten' tonnage. The report's own authors note that the edible-only share is substantially lower and that consumer-level waste is only one segment of the total.

The trace verdict: the number is real but the sentence is wrong. What the source supports: 35–40% of the food supply *by weight* is unsold or uneaten *including inedible parts* — bones, peels, pits — across the entire chain from farm to table. What the campaign version claims: 40% of food 'produced is never eaten,' which a normal reader hears as edible meals thrown away. Those are very different claims, and the difference is entirely in the methodology appendix that nobody in the chain quoted.

Three upgrades happened in transmission: a range (35–40) hardened into a point (40); 'by weight including inedible parts' dropped away; and a supply-chain total became a vague indictment that readers usually pin on household behavior, though consumer waste is only one segment. The honest citation: 'an estimated 35–40% of the food supply by weight goes unsold or uneaten when inedible parts are included.' Less punchy — and actually true. When a statistic survives only by losing its methodology, the methodology was the story.
A parenting blog told me playing classical music makes babies smarter — 'the Mozart effect.' My sister says that's not what the study found. Who's right?
Your sister has the better prior here, but let's do the trace rather than settle it by vibes:

arguments.query: Mozart effect original study what was tested students

messages.name: web_search
messages.content:
1. Parenting blog: 'Studies prove classical music boosts babies' brain development!' Cites 'the famous Mozart effect research.'
2. Psychology magazine explainer: traces the claim to a 1993 study and notes the popular version drifted far from it.
3. Original study abstract (1993, scientific journal): 36 college students listened to 10 minutes of a Mozart sonata, a relaxation tape, or silence, then took a spatial reasoning test; the Mozart group scored higher on that one test type, an effect lasting about 10–15 minutes.
One more check — what happened when other researchers tried to reproduce and extend it:

arguments.query: Mozart effect replication meta-analysis spatial reasoning temporary

messages.name: web_search
messages.content: Meta-analysis summary: across many follow-up studies, the effect shrank to small and short-lived, specific to certain spatial tasks, and partly attributable to arousal/mood (any enjoyable stimulus produced similar brief gains). No studies in the literature tested infants; child-development reviews describe the baby-products industry built on the claim as unsupported.

Your sister is right, and the trace shows the full anatomy of the drift. Original finding (1993): 36 *college students*, one spatial-reasoning test, a small improvement lasting *10–15 minutes* after 10 minutes of Mozart. What the claim became: classical music makes *babies* permanently *smarter*. Every load-bearing word changed — the population (adults → infants), the outcome (one spatial subtest → general intelligence), and the duration (minutes → development).

The replication record makes it worse for the blog: later work found the effect small, brief, and largely explained by mood — a story or a snack the students enjoyed worked about as well. And the meta-analysis confirms the decisive point: no study ever tested babies at all. The infant-products industry was built on a study of adults.

Verdict for your family chat: playing music you enjoy around your baby is lovely and harmless; the claim that it raises intelligence traces to a 1993 study that says nothing of the kind. When someone cites 'the Mozart effect,' the three questions that dismantle it are: who was studied, what was measured, and how long did it last?

Our office newsletter says 'research shows it takes 23 minutes to refocus after every interruption.' I emailed the editor and she said she got it from a productivity blog, which cited an HR magazine, which cited 'studies at a university.' Nobody seems to have the actual paper. Should I just let it go?

Don't let it go — but you don't need the paper to assess it, because the shape of what you found is itself the finding. Let me walk the chain you uncovered:

Newsletter → productivity blog → HR magazine → 'studies at a university.' That's three retellings and zero citations. Each hop is a place where qualifiers die: in chains like this, the original typically measured something narrow — say, the average time before people *returned* to an interrupted task in one workplace study, which includes time spent on other work in between — and by the third retelling it has become a universal constant about 'refocusing' after 'every interruption,' applied to a phone glance and a fire alarm alike.

Three specific reasons to distrust this instance:
1. The suspicious precision. '23 minutes' (often quoted as 23:15) has the texture of a single study's average being treated as a law of nature. Real refocusing varies enormously by task and interruption type.
2. The unattributed plural. 'Studies at a university' names nothing checkable. Genuine findings have authors, years, and journals; chains that end in fog usually started as something modest.
3. The definitional slide. Time-to-return-to-task, time-to-full-concentration, and time lost are three different measurements that all collapse into 'refocus' by the newsletter stage.

What to do: reply to the editor with the chain itself — 'this traces blog → magazine → unnamed studies; no primary source located' — and suggest the newsletter either find the paper (authors, year, what was actually measured, in whom) or soften the line to 'interruptions carry a real refocusing cost.' You're not claiming the number is false; you're showing it is *unowned*. No one in the chain will defend it, because no one in the chain ever saw the evidence. That's the tell, and it's worth teaching the whole office.

A wellness account I follow says 'science proves a coffee nap is 40% more effective than coffee or napping alone.' I asked for the source and they sent me a screenshot of another post, which mentions 'a Japanese study.' That's all I've got. Assess.

Assessment based on the chain you've got — and the chain is nearly the whole story:

What you hold: a claim ('40% more effective'), a screenshot of another post (a copy, not a source), and a nationality ('a Japanese study'). Notice what each element is doing. The precise percentage performs rigor; the screenshot performs citation; the country performs authority. None of the three is evidence.

What a real trace would need, and what I can tell you about the shape of this literature without the paper in hand: the coffee-nap studies that do exist are small laboratory experiments — typically a few dozen participants, a driving simulator or alertness test battery, one specific protocol (coffee immediately before a ~20-minute nap). In studies like that, '40%' would refer to one score on one test at one time point, not to 'effectiveness' in general — and small samples produce big, unstable percentages that shrink on replication.

So the claim fails at three checkpoints:
1. No paper, authors, or year — nothing to verify, by design or by sloppiness.
2. The metric is undefined: 40% more effective *at what, measured how, when?* A number without a denominator is decoration.
3. Even if the underlying study is real, a small simulator study cannot carry a blanket claim about your workday, your patients, or your driving.

Practical verdict: coffee naps are low-risk and plausibly helpful — you don't need the 40% to try one. But as a *cited fact* it's unusable, and the account's response to a source request (a screenshot of another post) tells you their standard of evidence. When the chain ends in a screenshot, the research answer is: claim unowned, treat as folklore until someone produces authors, year, and the test that was measured.

Our library newsletter states 'the average paperback novel contains about 90,000 words (industry data).' I'm on the library board and asked where that's from. The trail: the newsletter writer got it from a writers' forum sticky post; the sticky cites 'publishing industry standards'; I found the identical sentence on a print-on-demand company's help page, where it's used to estimate printing costs. No survey, no dataset anywhere. How should the board handle it?

You've completed a textbook trace, and the endpoint you found — a print-on-demand help page — explains everything about the number's career. Analysis:

1. What the number actually is at its origin: a *pricing heuristic*. A print-on-demand company needs a typical book length to estimate page counts and printing costs, so it publishes a round, plausible figure. For that purpose, precision doesn't matter and nobody checks it. The number was never a measurement; it was an assumption with a job.
2. How it got promoted: the writers' forum sticky quoted it as 'industry standards' (the company's page *is* industry, technically — that's the laundering step), and the newsletter completed the promotion to 'industry data,' a phrase that implies a dataset no one has ever seen.
3. Why it's probably not even accurate as an average: 'paperback novel' spans 60,000-word category romances and 200,000-word epic fantasies; any single average hides a distribution so wide that the average describes almost no actual book. A real figure would need a defined population (all novels published in a year? bestsellers? one genre?) and nobody in this chain defined one.

Recommendation for the board: this is a low-stakes claim, so the fix is cheap and worth doing as a matter of standards — either delete the parenthetical '(industry data),' which is the only false part, or replace the sentence with something the library can stand behind ('most of the novels on our new-fiction shelf run 250–400 pages'). The deeper point to minute for the board: the phrase 'industry data' should never survive editing unless the editor can name the dataset. Your trace — newsletter → forum → vendor help page — is a perfect training example: every hop sounded more authoritative while the underlying evidence stayed exactly zero.
A county health pamphlet says 'structured walking programs reduce fall risk in seniors by 31%.' Before our senior center builds a program around that number, verify it.
A program decision riding on one number — that earns a full trace to bedrock:

arguments.query: "reduce fall risk" walking program seniors "31%" pamphlet

messages.name: web_search
messages.content:
1. County health pamphlet (2025): 'Research shows structured walking programs reduce fall risk in seniors by 31%.' Source line: 'Journal of Community Health Studies, 2022.'
2. Community-health blog: repeats the 31% figure, citing the same journal article.
The pamphlet at least names a journal and year — that's checkable. Pulling the article:

arguments.query: Journal of Community Health Studies 2022 walking program fall risk seniors

messages.name: web_search
messages.content: Journal site: article exists (2022) — 'Community walking interventions and fall outcomes in older adults,' a narrative review. The 31% appears in its abstract, attributed to 'a 2019 conference presentation (Osei & Lindqvist).' The review's own body text describes the evidence base for walking programs as 'small and heterogeneous' and reports pooled estimates ranging from no effect to modest reductions.
The chain has one link left — the conference presentation the review's abstract relied on:

arguments.query: Osei Lindqvist 2019 conference walking falls older adults abstract

messages.name: web_search
messages.content: Conference proceedings archive: abstract located. It reports a pilot program with 38 participants over 10 weeks; the 31% is a reduction in a balance-test score (not in falls), presented as a preliminary result. No full paper by these authors on this program appears in the journal literature; the proceedings note 'full results to follow.'

Trace complete — and the chain ends at bedrock that isn't there. Full anatomy:

Pamphlet: 'walking programs reduce fall risk by 31%.' → Journal review's *abstract*: attributes 31% to a conference talk (while the review's own body calls the evidence small and heterogeneous — the pamphlet read the abstract, not the paper). → Conference abstract: a 38-person, 10-week pilot where 31% was an improvement in a *balance-test score*, not a reduction in falls — and the full results were never published, so the number was never peer-reviewed as a finished finding.

Three mutations: balance-score improvement became fall-risk reduction; a 38-person pilot became 'research shows'; an unpublished preliminary result became a county pamphlet's foundation. Verdict for the senior center: do not build the program's promises around 31%. Walking programs for seniors are low-risk and plausibly beneficial for strength and confidence, and the review does support 'modest, uncertain benefits' — pitch the program on that honest basis, measure your own participants' outcomes, and if anyone asks about 31%, you now know more about that number than the pamphlet's author did.
A pet store ad says '97% of pet owners consider their pet a member of the family.' My kid asked if that's really true. Trace it.
Good question from your kid — let's trace it the way we'd want her to:

arguments.query: "97%" pet owners "member of the family" survey

messages.name: web_search
messages.content:
1. Pet retail chain's campaign page: '97% of pet owners consider their pet family.' Small print: 'based on a 2024 survey.'
2. Pet industry magazine: repeats 97%, cites 'a 2024 national survey of pet owners.'
3. Survey firm's press release (2024): '97% of respondents agreed their pet is part of the family.'
The press release is the end of the public chain — now its methodology, which is where this kind of number is decided:

arguments.query: pet owner survey 2024 methodology online panel respondents sample

messages.name: web_search
messages.content: Survey methodology note: online opt-in panel of 1,050 adults who own pets, recruited from the survey firm's standing panel; respondents answered agree/disagree statements, including 'My pet is part of my family.' The survey was commissioned by a pet products association.

Here's the honest answer for your kid. The 97% is a real result of a real survey — nobody invented it. But look at who was asked and how: people who *already own pets*, who *volunteered for an online panel*, agreeing with a warm statement ('my pet is part of my family') that costs nothing to agree with. Ask pet owners if their pet is family and nearly all say yes — the survey mostly measured how the question was framed and who was in the room.

What it doesn't show: anything about non-owners, anything about behavior (spending, vet care, what people do when keeping the pet gets hard), and the sponsor — a pet products association — benefits from the warm glow. The claim also got stronger in the retelling: the survey says 97% *of its respondents agreed with a statement*; the ad says 97% of *pet owners* consider their pet family, full stop.

So: 'really true' in the narrow sense — yes, that survey got that result. True as a fact about the world — it's closer to 'pet owners who take surveys love their pets,' which your kid probably could have told us without a panel. That's the lesson worth teaching: a percentage always has a 'of whom, asked what, by whom' hiding inside it.
I found two spec sheets for the AquaPure 3000 water softener — one says grain capacity 32,000, the other says 40,000. Which is right? Files are aquapure-3000-spec-a.pdf and aquapure-3000-spec-b.pdf.

Conflicting spec sheets are settled by the documents themselves — dates, revision tables, and supersession notes — not by which one ranks higher or looks newer. Reading both, and I'll go straight to the parts people skip: footers and revision histories.

messages.name: file_read
messages.content:
AquaPure 3000 — Specification Sheet
Grain capacity: 32,000 grains. Resin volume: 1.0 cu ft. Flow rate: 11 gpm. Salt capacity: 220 lb.
[Footer] Document AP-SPEC-3000, Rev. C — March 2019. Supersedes Rev. B (2017).

messages.name: file_read
messages.content:
AquaPure 3000 — Specification Sheet
Grain capacity: 40,000 grains. Resin volume: 1.25 cu ft. Flow rate: 12 gpm. Salt capacity: 260 lb.
Revision history: Rev. F — June 2025 (resin tank enlarged; capacities updated). Rev. E — 2023 (control valve change). Rev. D — 2021 (editorial). Rev. C — 2019.
[Footer] Document AP-SPEC-3000, Rev. F — June 2025. This revision supersedes all previous revisions.

Settled by the documents' own machinery: spec B is Rev. F (June 2025) and its revision history explains the discrepancy — the resin tank was enlarged in 2025, raising grain capacity from 32,000 to 40,000. Spec A is Rev. C (2019), explicitly superseded. So for a unit manufactured now, 40,000 grains is correct.

One important refinement: 'which is right' depends on which physical unit you have. If you're speccing a replacement part or checking an *existing* installation from before 2025, the 2019 sheet may describe your actual hardware — the revision history (tank enlarged at Rev. F) is the dividing line. Check the unit's manufacture date or serial against that.

The general rule this demonstrates: when two versions of a document conflict, never decide by filename, file date, or search ranking. Open both and read the footer and the revision table — manufacturers maintain that apparatus precisely so this question has an answer, and the revision history often tells you *why* the number changed, which is what turns a contradiction into information.
I found a page saying the homestead tax exemption filing deadline here is March 1. The page has no date on it anywhere. Can I rely on it?

An undated page stating a deadline gets no trust on its own — deadlines are exactly the kind of fact that changes. The procedure: treat it as an unverified claim and try to corroborate it against a dated, authoritative source. If corroboration fails, we drop it, however plausible it sounds.

arguments.query: county tax assessor homestead exemption filing deadline

messages.name: web_search
messages.content:
1. County tax assessor's official page (page footer: 'Last updated November 2026'): 'Homestead exemption applications must be filed by March 1 of the tax year.' Links the application form and the statute reference.
2. County newspaper article (Jan 2026): reminds residents of the March 1 homestead deadline, quoting the assessor's office.

Corroborated — and notice what the corroboration consisted of. The assessor's own page, carrying a 'last updated November 2026' footer, states the same March 1 deadline, and a January 2026 newspaper reminder independently agrees. Two dated sources, one of them the administering office, matching the undated page's claim.

So you can rely on March 1 — but understand what you're relying on: not the undated page (which earned nothing), but the assessor's current page that happens to confirm it. If the two had disagreed, the undated page would have been discarded without a second thought, because an undated source cannot win an argument against a dated authority — it can't even establish which year's rule it describes.

Habit to keep: for any undated page, ask 'what would this look like if it were five years old and wrong?' If the page would look exactly the same, it carries no evidence about the present. Dates aren't pedantry; they're what make a statement about a changing world checkable.

This safety data sheet for our workshop solvent shows 'updated March 2026' in the search result, so it's current, right? The file is solvent-sds.pdf — check it before we rely on the first-aid section.

That 'updated' stamp in a search result usually dates the *web page or file upload*, not the document's content — a classic trap with PDFs that get re-hosted. The document's own revision apparatus is the authority. Reading the file's header, footer, and revision sections directly:

messages.name: file_read
messages.content:
SAFETY DATA SHEET — Solvent K-9 Industrial Cleaner
Section 1: Identification. Supplier: Kline Chemical.
Section 4: First aid measures. [Text as issued.]
...
Section 16: Other information. Date of issue: 14 June 2022. Revision number: 3. 'This SDS replaces the version dated 2019.' Preparation information: prepared by the supplier's regulatory department.
[Document footer] SDS-K9-EN Rev. 3 — 2022.

Your skepticism was warranted: the document itself says it was issued 14 June 2022, revision 3 — the March 2026 date in the search result is when the file was uploaded or re-indexed on the hosting site, not when its content was revised. Nothing inside the document supports a 2026 revision; the supplier's regulatory department prepared a 2022 document and the web has been carrying it ever since.

Practical consequences: the first-aid and hazard content may still be accurate — 2022 isn't ancient for a stable product — but you cannot tell a safety auditor (or yourself) that you're working from the current SDS. The correct next step is to request the latest revision from Kline Chemical directly and compare revision numbers; suppliers are obliged to provide current SDSs, and if a Rev. 4 exists with changed first-aid guidance, the 2022 copy in your binder is a liability.

Rule of thumb from this case: for PDFs, the only dates that count are the ones *inside* the document — issue date, revision number, supersession line. Search-result dates, file timestamps, and 'last modified' headers date the container, never the content.

For our grant application I wrote 'average rent for a two-bedroom here is $1,150, per a housing report.' The report is from 2018. The grant reviewer will just check the citation exists, right? It's probably close enough.

Two problems, and 'close enough' is the smaller one.

First, the substantive problem: rents are one of the fastest-moving numbers in local data.
